senses.gloss:
Talāśa is the name of a tree in the Atharvaveda. Whitney suggests that it may be the same as tālīśa (Flacourtia cataphracta).
Foot notes vi. 15, 3.
Translation of the Atharvaveda, 291.
Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 62.

Talpa is the regular term for ‘bed’ or ‘couch’ from the Rigveda and the Atharvaveda onwards. One made of udumbara wood is mentioned in the taittirīya brāhmaṇa. The violation of the bed of a Guru, or teacher, is already mentioned in the Chāndogya upaniṣad, while the adjective talpya, ‘born in the nuptial couch,’ denotes ‘legitimate’ in the Śatapatha brāhmaṇa.
Foot notes Rv. vii. 55, 8; Av. v. 17, 12; xiv. 2, 31. 41.
taittirīya Saṃhitā, vi. 2, 6, 4; taittirīya brāhmaṇa, ii. 2, 5, 3; pañcaviṃśa brāhmaṇa, xxiii. 4, 2; xxv. 1, 10.
i. 2, 6, 5.
v. 10, 9.
xiii. 1, 6, 2. Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 154.

Talava in the list of victims at the Puruṣamedha, or human sacrifice, in the yajurveda, denotes a ‘musician’ of some kind.
Foot notes Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 20; taittirīya brāhmaṇa, iii. 4, 15, 1. Cf. Weber, Indische Streifen, 1, 83, n. 15.
